figures.caption: Fig. 1. Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC) matrix revealing multicollinearity patterns in the HEA dataset. The heatmap displays intercorrelations among compo­ sitional and physical characteristics, with correlation coefficients ranging from −1 to +1. Several elemental features exhibit strong positive correlations (r>0.8), demonstrating redundant information that necessitated feature engineering approaches. Feature descriptions are provided in Table S4. 5

Fig. 2. Predicted versus actual thermal expansion coefficient values for machine learning models on the test dataset. (a) ANN demonstrates a strong correlation (R2 = 0.9052, RMSE = 1.3254), (b) SVR with competitive performance (R2 = 0.8663, RMSE = 1.5742), (c) XGBR demonstrating consistent generalization (R2 = 0.8967, RMSE = 1.3835), and (d) RFR with conservative performance (R2 = 0.8773, RMSE = 1.5080). The dashed line represents perfect prediction (y = x), with data points closer to this line indicating better model accuracy.

Fig. 3. Convergence behavior of active learning (AL) frameworks for CTE minimization in high-entropy alloys (HEAs). Mean convergence trajectories over 100 independent optimization runs are shown for (a) Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) and (b) Random Forest Variance (RFV) surrogate models using Expected Improvement (EI) and Lower Confidence Bound (LCB) acquisition functions. Solid lines denote the mean coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE), while shaded regions represent the 10–90 percentile range across all runs, illustrating both convergence speed and robustness.

Fig. 4. Exploration–exploitation patterns in AL for CTE minimization using different surrogate model and acquisition function combinations. The spatial distribution of sampling points reveals distinct optimization strategies: (a) GPR with EI showing distributed exploration across the search space, (b) GPR with LCB demonstrating concentrated exploitation in promising low-CTE regions after approximately 50 iterations, (c) RFV with EI maintaining progressive exploration throughout optimiza­ tion cycles, and (d) RFV with LCB exhibiting focused sampling density in optimal zones. EI-based approaches maintain broader spatial exploration even in later cycles, while LCB strategies transition to concentrated exploitation once favorable regions are identified.

Fig. 5. Simple regret comparison between AL approaches and CMA-ES evo­ lutionary strategy throughout the optimization process. The solid lines show mean simple regret across 100 runs, with shaded regions representing the 25th- 75th percentile range. CMA-ES consistently exhibits higher simple regret levels compared to both GPR-EI and GPR-LCB approaches. The active learning meth­ ods demonstrate superior consistency with significantly lower variability in solution quality, as evidenced by their standard deviations (GPR-LCB: 0.009, GPR-EI: 0.020) compared to CMA-ES (0.075), highlighting the exceptional sta­ bility and reliability of the AL framework for materials discovery applications where consistency is critical for resource-intensive validation processes.

Fig. 6. Convergence characteristics of the MFAL framework for HEA composi­ tion optimization targeting minimal CTE. The black line represents the average best performance across independent runs, with the shaded region indicating the ±1 std. dev. region. The framework demonstrates robust convergence behav­ ior, achieving near-optimal solutions within approximately 75 iterations. The consistent convergence pattern across multiple runs highlights the framework’s effectiveness in navigating the complex compositional space of high-entropy al­ loys while maintaining computational efficiency through multi-fidelity sampling strategies. (For interpretation of the references to colour in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the web version of this article.)

Fig. 7. Single-run convergence dynamics of the MFAL framework illustrating the strategic balance between high and low-fidelity data points. The plot displays the best thermal expansion coefficient (CTE) values achieved over iterations, demonstrating characteristic step-wise improvement patterns that reflect the algorithm’s strategic learning process. The framework intelligently alternates between high-fidelity evaluations for exploitation of promising regions and low- fidelity sampling for exploration of the broader compositional landscape. This dual-fidelity approach enables efficient information gathering while maintaining consistent solution quality improvements throughout the optimization process.

Fig. 8. Convergence comparison between MFAL and single-fidelity active learn­ ing at 1:20 cost ratio. MFAL achieves 56.4% cost reduction while maintaining comparable solution quality. Solid lines show mean values across 100 runs and the shaded regions indicate 10th-90th percentile range.

Fig. 9. Evolution of optimal alloy compositions, radar plots showing the progression of the best-found alloy compositions at iterations 5, 20, 40, and 60 for three methods: GPR-EI, GPR-LCB, and MFAL. Each axis represents the normalized fraction of the six alloying elements (Fe, Ni, Co, Cr, V, Cu) in the optimal composition identified at each iteration. The CTE values (×10−6 𝐾−1) for the best compositions are shown in the legends. Plots demonstrate the convergence behavior of different acquisition functions, with all methods converging to similar low-CTE compositions characterized by high Fe content and reduced fractions of other elements. Notably, the best value found and optimal composition remain largely unchanged after approximately 60 iterations. 11

GPR-LCB demonstrates superior cumulative regret performance (81.38) com- pared to GPR-EI (95.74), indicating a 15% improvement in optimization eﬃciency with fewer wasted iterations on inferior compositions.
